The post-metamorphic juvenile then enters a period of rapid somatic growth, during which the shell expands considerably as the animal actively grazes on periphyton and decaying plant matter. Growth rates in this species are highly temperature-dependent, with development proceeding slowly under cool conditions. The ecological consequence of this thermal suppression is that populations in northern or high-altitude habitats may experience severely constrained breeding seasons, limiting annual recruitment to brief windows of warmer weather.

When the thermal regime shifts upward, the reproductive output of this freshwater gastropod increases dramatically.
